background.text: It's a completely unprecedented time in America, and we are right in the, not just witnessing history, but we're right in the middle of history, and I think we're at a turning point. background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: I know, Governor, that you've praised Baltimore's police, as well as its residents, for holding peaceful protests. But I'm sure you remember just a few years ago, after the death of Freddie Gray, Baltimore erupted into violence. What do you think has changed between then and now?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, I remember it very well. I had just been governor for 90 days when we had the worst violence in 47 years break out in our largest city. It was quite a different situation than what we experienced this time. In the first few hours, we had 400 businesses and homes burned and looted and destroyed and 137 police and firefighters injured. And the city was overwhelmed and out of control. We learned a lot from that. And I think five years later, we've made a lot of progress, both on the side of the police department and on the community who said, we don't want to see that violence. We don't want to burn down our own city. I was really proud of the citizens of Baltimore. It was thousands of people came out and peacefully protested. Look, we certainly have by no means solved all the problems of Baltimore or in police departments. We have taken some really big steps and made some real progress. First of all, we passed criminal justice reform in our state, the most aggressive in America. We did it before the federal bill was passed and they modeled it on what we did here in Maryland. We lowered our prison population by more than 49 other states in the country. We lowered sentences for many different crimes other than violent crimes, which is still a problem. And, you know, 90 percent of the citizens in Baltimore. Want want us to get tough on violent crimes.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: Governor Hogan, as you well know, there have been suggestions for defunding the police, really taking a lot of that money, if not all of it, and investing more in communities, in social services and programs. What do you think of that idea, and do you have any plans to consider it?

ground_truth: I think the idea of defunding or reducing funding for police is a terrible idea. We've been able to improve things by investing more in our police, in recruitment, in training, in equipment, trying to teach people about de-escalation. We've got a very diverse police department. That's majority, minority, and I think they're better equipped, better trained, body cameras. They spend a lot of time in the community working with folks and I think it's really helped. The problems are not solved by any means, don't get me wrong. But there's a little bit more trust and a little bit more communication and spending more time listening to the concerns and trying to work together is what it's really all about. The second part of the question about investing more into some of the other areas, we've been investing record funding into our schools and more money into the social programs. I think you've got to do both. You've got to invest in those communities and give people more opportunities and you've got to help with some of the underlying needs of those communities. I think the first part of the question about investing more into some of the other areas, we've been investing record funding into our schools and socioeconomic problems but eliminating or defunding police is not the way.

background.text: You were on the call when President Trump told the governors that they looked weak and needed to dominate, his words, not mine, the protesters. What was your reaction at that moment, Governor Hogan?

ground_truth: First, I thought it was that was the wrong way to go about it. I thought it was terrible the way they moved in on those protesters. background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: As Maryland continues to reopen, I know you're getting some pressure from businesses to open even further and faster. What are we learning about the virus' spread and what are you most concerned, not only about reopening, but when it comes to protesting?

ground_truth: So on the reopening, we, as chair of the National Governors Association, we kind of wrote a book, gave guidelines. NGA put out a guideline for all the governors about a safe and effective reopening. Here in Maryland, we brought together some of the smartest doctors and scientists from across not only our state, but in America, from places like Johns Hopkins and the University of Maryland Medical System. We have a really safe and effective gradual reopening because we need to get our economy back on track. But we've also completely flattened the curve. We've dropped our positivity rate by more than 70 percent, and we're going to continue to slowly and safely reopen things. It's a balancing act because you want to make sure that you get people back to work, that we help our small businesses, but that we don't cause that spike. And so there's some pressure to reopen, but, you know, Washington Post poll just said 85 percent of the people in our state approve of the job we've done on the reopening. So I'm just going to keep doing it gradually. We are concerned about the protesters. I know that Scott Gottlieb, the former F.D.A. commissioner, said, you know, about two and a half times more chance of getting the virus by being out there in those protests. Just a week or two ago, we had 10 person limits on gatherings and now we have 10,000 people gathering. So we're going to encourage everyone who was involved with those thousands of people to go out and get tested. It's a concern of all the governors across America that we want to make sure people express their frustrations, but we don't want them getting sick and spreading the virus.

background.text: How concerned are you about the unemployment rate and so many people being out of jobs? I mean, it's still a dire situation. What can you do about that in the state?

ground_truth: It's the biggest thing that I'm worried about right now.
